messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Michael was twenty-three when the abuse began, and he was already a patrol officer, already trained to read threat in the flicker of a muscle. His partner, a woman he had been with for nearly two years, had never raised a hand before the night she came home from a bar reeking of cheap whiskey and accused him of hiding something. He tried to calm her, and she swung. The first punch caught him across the jaw; the second, as he turned, landed on his kidney. He did not fight back. He was a cop. He knew how these calls went. He stayed still, let it happen, and when she finally stumbled into the bedroom, he sat on the couch for hours, pressing a bag of frozen peas to his ribs and listening to his own breathing. That single night, he told himself, would be the end. It was not. Over the next fourteen months she hit him, shoved him, threw glass at him, and once locked him in the bathroom for six hours. He never reported it. He believed he could manage it, contain it, keep it separate from the job. But what he could not contain was the way his own body began to remember things he did not want recalled.

Now he is twenty-six, a detective in a busy precinct, and he is married to a different woman—someone gentle, patient, a teacher who leaves sticky notes on his coffee mug. He loves her, but he cannot let her touch him without flinching. Any form of physical contact—a hand on his shoulder, a hug from behind—sends a spike of cold through his chest, and he has learned to step sideways, to pivot, to keep distance. He tells himself it is better that way. Safer. He has also stopped relaxing. After work, he used to sit on the back porch with a book; now he cannot. Relaxing feels dangerous, like lowering a shield in enemy territory, so he stays upright, stays alert, watching the door. He has come to believe that people are not what they seem—that the person you trust can become the person who hurts you without warning. That belief has hardened into a kind of permanent suspicion, a feeling that he is an outsider now, set apart from the ordinary trust that other people share. He lost faith in people, in the idea that the world is predictable or fair. He does not pray anymore, though he used to.

His memories of the abuse are relentlessly clear and detailed. He can still see the pattern in the linoleum floor as he lay on his side. He can hear the sound of her voice, the exact pitch of the accusations, the scrape of a chair leg. The memory forces its way into his mind during quiet moments—at his desk, in the car, in the four a.m. stillness of his own kitchen—and when it comes, he sometimes hears the sounds again, the thud of a fist against drywall, the shatter of a bottle. The auditory recall is so vivid that he will jerk upright, certain the noise was real.

At work, the triggers are constant. He is the first officer at a domestic call, and the smell of alcohol on a suspect’s breath sends a wave of nausea coiling through his stomach. He sees visible injuries on a victim—a split lip, a bruise blooming along a jawline—and he has to excuse himself to the restroom, where he breathes into his palms until the shaking passes. He has learned to numb his feelings deliberately, to seal them off behind a professional flatness that his colleagues mistake for composure. But that numbness leaks into his marriage. His wife has started to ask why he never seems present, why he flinches, why he refuses to sit still on the couch with her. He does not tell her. He cannot. The words would require him to admit what happened, to own the shame of being a man who could not protect himself.

He is seeking help now because his captain noticed the way he went pale at a crime scene and quietly recommended a therapist. Michael came because he was told to, but also because something is wearing thin. He is tired of the vigilance, the nausea, the way his own mind ambushes him. He is afraid of what he might become if this goes on—afraid that the outsider he feels himself turning into will eventually be all that is left. He wants to stop flinching when his wife reaches for him. He does not know if that is possible, but he walked into the office anyway, and that is more than he has done in three years.
